My research sits at the intersection of **energy and environmental policy, public opinion, behavioural science and environmental psychology**. Across projects, I examine how people interpret policy problems, evaluate technologies and trade-offs, respond to environmental risks, and form preferences about collective responses.

## Research themes

::: {.card-grid}
::: {.research-card}
<div class="card-icon">A</div>

### Public acceptance of emerging energy technologies

I study how people evaluate low-carbon technologies and infrastructure, with particular attention to hydrogen, ammonia, offshore renewable energy, perceived risks and benefits, and the conditions under which public support changes.
:::

::: {.research-card}
<div class="card-icon">B</div>

### Climate risk, extreme weather & behaviour

This work examines how direct experience, perceived harm, information seeking and social interaction shape preparedness, community helping, climate action and support for mitigation and adaptation policies.
:::

::: {.research-card}
<div class="card-icon">C</div>

### Energy policy, knowledge & social identity

A third strand investigates the relationship between public knowledge, values, political and social identities, and preferences for energy, water and resource-management policies.
:::
:::

## Ocean-REFuel {#ocean-refuel}

**University of Bath · EPSRC-funded interdisciplinary programme**

Ocean-REFuel investigates the potential to convert ocean renewable energy into liquid and gaseous zero-carbon fuels, including hydrogen and ammonia. Within this broader programme, my work focuses on the **social and behavioural dimensions of future energy systems**: public attitudes, acceptance, perceived risks and benefits, policy rationales, and the ways communities evaluate proposed energy developments.

The project brings together researchers across engineering, psychology, policy and economics, with the University of Strathclyde as lead institution and collaborators including Bath, Cardiff, Imperial College London, Nottingham and Newcastle.

[Ocean-REFuel project website](https://www.oceanrefuel.ac.uk/) · [University of Bath project page](https://researchportal.bath.ac.uk/en/projects/ocean-refuel-ocean-renewable-energy-fuels-2/)

## Methods

My research combines **quantitative, experimental, qualitative and mixed-method approaches**. I am especially interested in designs that can identify how people make trade-offs, how attitudes are structured, and how evidence can inform policy design and public engagement.

::: {.method-grid}
::: {.method-card}
### Surveys & experiments
Survey design and implementation · choice-based conjoint analysis · randomised controlled trials · programme evaluation.
:::
::: {.method-card}
### Statistical modelling
Structural equation modelling · path analysis · cluster and factor analysis · OLS, logistic, ordinal and multinomial regression · fixed-, random- and mixed-effects models.
:::
::: {.method-card}
### Quasi-experimental methods
Instrumental variables · regression discontinuity · difference-in-differences.
:::
::: {.method-card}
### Qualitative & mixed methods
Interviews · focus groups · deliberative workshops · ethnographic fieldwork · interpretative phenomenological analysis · discourse analysis · grounded theory · participatory rural appraisal.
:::
:::

<div class="skill-strip"><strong>Software:</strong> Stata · SPSS · AMOS · Excel · R · Python · NVivo</div>

## Earlier research

My earlier work includes energy efficiency policy preferences, public energy literacy, water-policy knowledge, the social-identity foundations of energy and water policy preferences, and behavioural responses following the 2020 Oregon wildfires. Before specialising in environmental and energy policy, I also published on political trust, governance, public policy, policing and political development in Pakistan.
